newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Fokker rescue talks fail - administrators.
newsitem.headline: Fokker rescue talks fail - administrators.

text.p: Court-appointed administrators at Dutch planemaker Fokker said on Thursday that they had ended possible rescue talks with South Korea's Samsung Aerospace after Shorts had said that it would no longer supply wings for Fokker aircraft.
"Administrators are therefore forced to conclude that a re-launch of Fokker on the basis of continuing current production is no longer feasible," they said in a statement.
Administrators said there was very little chance of an alternative rescue plan going ahead with another supplier of wings.
"The chances that the Fokker (aircraft) programme could survive on the basis of such a plan are minimal," they said in a statement.
"It goes without saying that Fokker...will continue to make aircraft already ordered by KLM Cityhopper, Vietnam Airlines and Ethiopian Airlines," they said.
The administrators said that under an agreement with Fokker suppliers, they had been able to keep open supply lines from firms such as Shorts until October 31.
Although talks with Samsung had initially made good progress they had run into delays in late October, administrators said.

"As a result, the crucial date of October 31 passed without orders being placed with suppliers and without a memorandum of understanding on a "new" Fokker between Samsung, the (Dutch) state, Stork and administrators."
In July Stork bought Fokker's profitable maintenance activities.
The administrators said that Samsung had informed them earlier on Thursday that they would need another month to decide on whether to take over Fokker.
They said they had tried to extend the supply agreement with supplier firms, but Shorts had said it was no longer prepared to provide wings for Fokker's F-70 and F-100 jets.

Other suppliers had said that the high costs of re-launching Fokker production would have to be charged to Fokker, but Samsung had said it was not prepared to take on the additional costs brought about by delays in making a final decision.
Fokker was declared bankrupt on March 15

Founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, it had become one of the world's largest planemakers by 1928, going on to develop 125 different aircraft, ranging from passenger planes to fighters and bombers.
But more recently Fokker struggled to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.
In 1987 the Dutch government baled it out and six years later Daimler-Benz AG's Deutsche Aerospace (DASA) paid 686 million guilders for a 51 percent stake in Fokker.

But despite job cuts and tight cost control, depressed world aircraft markets and a weak dollar saw the company steadily lose altitude and sink into deeper and deeper losses which had to be met by DASA and the Dutch government.
In January 1996, Daimler-Benz said it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses and cut off all financial support.
The Dutch government provided interim finance to keep Fokker alive while it completed outstanding orders for some 30 planes.
In the meantime administrators sought a powerful investor capable of hauling the core plane-making operations out of bankruptcy and make them a viable business.
Canada's Bombardier group initially emerged as a front-runner but ultimately baulked at the risks involved.

Samsung also indicated an interest at an early stage but soon withdrew from the scene. Hope seemed to be fading for Fokker when projects mooted by a Russian group and Dutch venture capitalists failed to get off the ground.
But Samsung re-emerged as a potential saviour in August and in September it was granted the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books with a view to a possible takeover.
In the interim, some of Fokker's profitable parts were sold off to raise money for creditors and buy more time while Fokker's bankrupt core completed the orders left on its books.
Samsung handed over a business plan for Fokker to the Dutch authorities on October 8 and official talks over a possible relaunch began on October 16.
The Korean firm was said to have been lured by Fokker's technical facilities and its research and development experience which it hoped to put to work on plans for a new 125-seater jet.
Fokker had previously focused on the short-to-medium haul airliner market with 50-, 70-, and 100-seater aircraft.
